content: Weeks 1–4 (Early pregnancy): At conception, a fertilised egg implants in the uterine wall. Hormones hCG, progesterone and oestrogen surge. Many women have no symptoms yet, but some notice a missed period, mild cramping, light spotting (implantation bleeding), breast tenderness, or fatigue. This is the time to start taking folic acid 400–800 mcg daily if you have not already, as it prevents neural tube defects in the first weeks of development.

Weeks 5–8: The embryo's heart begins beating around week 6. Morning sickness (nausea and vomiting) is very common and peaks around weeks 8–10. Breasts grow heavier and more tender. Fatigue is often severe. The embryo develops its basic organ systems. Tips for nausea: eat small, frequent meals, try dry crackers before getting out of bed, ginger tea, and stay hydrated. Avoid strong smells that trigger nausea.

Weeks 9–12 (End of first trimester): The embryo is now officially a foetus. Miscarriage risk drops significantly after week 10–12. Fingers and toes form; the baby starts moving (though you cannot feel it yet). Morning sickness may begin to ease. Your uterus grows to about the size of a grapefruit. A nuchal translucency ultrasound (NT scan) around week 11–13 screens for chromosomal conditions. Book your first prenatal appointment if you have not already — ideally before week 10.

Second trimester overview (weeks 13–27): Often called the 'honeymoon trimester'. Morning sickness usually fades, energy returns, and the bump becomes visible. The baby develops hearing (can recognise your voice), eyebrows, fingerprints, and begins swallowing amniotic fluid. You may feel the first fluttery baby movements (quickening) around weeks 16–20. Key appointments: anatomy scan at weeks 18–20 to check all organs and gender if desired; glucose screening at weeks 24–28 for gestational diabetes.

Weeks 13–16: The placenta fully takes over hormone production from the ovaries. The risk of miscarriage is now very low. Round ligament pain (sharp pains on the sides of the lower abdomen) is common as the uterus expands. You may notice increased appetite as nausea lifts. Skin changes are common — some women glow, others develop acne or the linea nigra (dark line on the abdomen). Vaginal discharge increases — this is normal unless it has a bad smell, is yellow/green, or itches.

Weeks 17–20: The anatomy scan (also called the 20-week scan or anomaly scan) takes place in this window. It checks all major organs, the spine, brain, heart, limbs, and placenta position. You can also find out the baby's sex if you want. Quickening (first felt movements) usually happens between weeks 16–22 for first-time mothers, or earlier for those who have been pregnant before. Movements feel like bubbles, flutters, or gentle taps.

Weeks 21–27: The baby reaches the viability milestone around week 24 — meaning with specialist care, a baby born now could survive. Baby gains weight rapidly, opens and closes eyes, and responds to light and sound. Braxton Hicks contractions (practice contractions) become more noticeable. Glucose tolerance test for gestational diabetes is done around week 24–28. Heartburn, back pain, and leg cramps are common complaints in this phase.

Third trimester overview (weeks 28–40): The final stretch. The baby doubles in weight and the brain develops rapidly. Movements may slow slightly as space gets tight — but you should still feel at least 10 movements per day. Common discomforts include swollen feet and ankles, shortness of breath, pelvic girdle pain, and difficulty sleeping. Prepare your hospital bag from week 36. Group B Strep (GBS) test is done around week 35–37.

Weeks 28–32: The baby's eyes open and close; it can taste and hear clearly. Rapid brain growth. Preterm labour risk increases — know the signs: regular contractions before week 37, pelvic pressure, unusual lower back pain, increased discharge, or fluid leaking. Sleep on your left side if possible — it improves blood flow to the baby. An iron and haemoglobin check is often done at this stage, as anaemia is common in the third trimester.

Weeks 33–36: The baby settles into a head-down position (vertex presentation) in preparation for birth, though some babies turn late. If breech (bottom-down) at week 36, your doctor may discuss an ECV (external cephalic version) to turn the baby, or plan a C-section. Pack your hospital bag and plan your route to the hospital. Colostrum (early milk) production often starts now — you may notice breast leaking.

Weeks 37–40 (Full term): The baby is fully formed and adding weight. Labour can begin any day. Signs of labour: regular contractions that intensify and get closer together, your waters breaking (a gush or steady trickle of clear fluid), a bloody show (mucus plug discharge). Go to hospital if contractions are 5 minutes apart for 1 hour, your waters break, you notice heavy bleeding, or the baby stops moving.

Warning signs in pregnancy — when to call your doctor or go to the emergency room immediately: heavy vaginal bleeding at any stage, severe abdominal pain or cramping, signs of preeclampsia (sudden severe headache, vision changes, upper right abdominal pain, significant face or hand swelling), high fever above 38.3°C / 101°F, difficulty breathing, reduced or no foetal movement after week 28, fluid leaking from the vagina before week 37, symptoms of a blood clot in the leg (one calf hot, swollen, and painful).

Safe exercise during pregnancy: For most healthy pregnancies, 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week is recommended (e.g. walking, swimming, prenatal yoga, cycling on a stationary bike). Exercise improves mood, reduces back pain, controls weight gain, and may make labour shorter. Avoid: contact sports (boxing, football), exercises with a fall risk (horse riding, skiing), lying flat on your back after the first trimester, high-altitude activities, and scuba diving. Always check with your doctor before starting a new exercise routine.

Common pregnancy discomforts and remedies: Heartburn — eat small frequent meals, avoid spicy/fatty foods, stay upright after eating, prop up your head in bed. Backache — wear flat shoes, sleep with a pillow between your knees, do gentle stretches, avoid heavy lifting. Swollen feet/ankles — elevate feet when resting, wear compression socks, stay hydrated, avoid standing for long periods. Leg cramps — stretch calf muscles before bed, stay hydrated, calcium and magnesium intake. Constipation — drink more water, eat fibre-rich foods (daal, vegetables, whole grain roti), walk daily.

Sleep during pregnancy: Sleeping on your left side is ideal after week 16 because it improves blood flow to the baby and kidneys. Use a pregnancy pillow or regular pillows for support — between the knees, under the belly, behind the back. If you wake on your back, simply roll back to your side. Short periods on your back are not dangerous; your body will signal discomfort if circulation is restricted. Avoid sleeping pills without doctor approval. For restless legs syndrome (a crawling sensation), stretching, magnesium, and staying hydrated can help.

Preeclampsia: A serious condition in pregnancy characterised by high blood pressure (above 140/90 mmHg) after week 20, combined with protein in the urine or other organ damage signs. Symptoms: severe headache, blurred or altered vision, upper right abdominal pain (just below the ribs), nausea/vomiting in the second half of pregnancy, sudden severe swelling of the face, hands, or feet. Preeclampsia can progress to eclampsia (seizures) and is life-threatening. If you experience these symptoms, go to hospital immediately. It is Pakistan's leading cause of maternal death.

Prenatal care appointments (Pakistan context): Ideally, attend at least 8 antenatal visits during pregnancy. Key milestones: First visit before 10 weeks (confirm pregnancy, blood tests, blood pressure, weight, general health), NT scan at 11–13 weeks, anatomy scan at 18–22 weeks, glucose test at 24–28 weeks, GBS swab at 35–37 weeks, weekly visits from week 36. Tests include: blood group & Rh factor, haemoglobin (anaemia is very common in Pakistan), blood pressure monitoring, urine for protein and infection, and foetal growth scans.

Gestational diabetes: A type of diabetes that develops during pregnancy because of hormonal changes that make cells less sensitive to insulin. It affects about 10–15% of pregnancies. It is diagnosed via a glucose tolerance test (GTT) at weeks 24–28. If diagnosed: monitor blood sugar, follow a low-glycaemic diet (reduce white rice, white bread, sugary drinks, sweets), eat small frequent meals, stay active, and take medication if your doctor prescribes it. Uncontrolled gestational diabetes can cause a very large baby (macrosomia), difficult delivery, and C-section risk.

Preparing for labour and birth: Signs that labour is approaching: the baby 'drops' lower into the pelvis (lightening), Braxton Hicks contractions become more frequent, you pass the mucus plug (thick, sometimes blood-streaked discharge), energy bursts (nesting instinct). When real labour starts: contractions are regular, get stronger and closer together, and do not stop when you move or rest. Pack your hospital bag by week 36: ID documents, hospital card, maternity notes, comfortable clothing, newborn clothes, breast pads, sanitary pads, snacks, phone charger.
